Reducing Order Sensitivity in Decision Models

Bodong Liu Affiliation: Department of Computer Science, Cornell University, New York, USA Correspondence to: bl576@cornell.edu    Dongyoung Go Affiliation: Department of Computer Science, Cornell University, New York, USA    Sofian Zalouk Affiliation: Department of Computer Science, Cornell University, New York, USA    Kilian Q. Weinberger Affiliation: Department of Computer Science, Cornell University, New York, USA
Abstract

Decision models are emerging as fast components of larger AI systems. Yet recent decision models, such as Jev, process options sequentially, leading to different predictions based on their ordering. Across ten open- and closed-source decision models, we find that order-sensitivity is pervasive, causing substantial accuracy degradation and unreliable decision-making. These effects become more pronounced as the number of options grows and can compound across multi-step decisions. To address this problem, we systematically compare eight methods for mitigating order sensitivity in terms of robustness, predictive accuracy, and inference efficiency. Among these methods, we find that tree attention is a surprisingly effective and efficient method. It achieves order invariance by processing options as parallel branches of a shared context. When used during training, it matches the baseline’s average accuracy. Applied to the baseline without retraining, it also eliminates order sensitivity with only a 1.1-point drop in accuracy. Our findings demonstrate that order invariance can be enforced directly in decision models with little or no loss in predictive accuracy.

Keywords: 
Machine Learning, order sensitivity, permutation invariance, positional bias, decision models

1 Introduction

Recently, decision models have gained popularity for fast and typed decisions (Almeida, 2026; OpenAI, 2026). Given a context (question) and a set of candidate options, a decision model returns a distribution over the given options in a single prefill pass. Therefore, they are well suited as lightweight components within larger systems, for example, routing documents, handling customer support, or choosing an agent’s next tool call (OpenAI, 2026; TypeSafe, 2026; Ling et al., 2026; Stefaniuk, 2026; Zhu et al., 2026a). However, simply presenting the same options in a different order can change their decisions, even when the order is semantically irrelevant, a weakness known as order sensitivity.

Order sensitivity has been widely studied in language models (Pezeshkpour & Hruschka, 2024; Zheng et al., 2023), but it remains under-researched for decision models, where its consequences are arguably more severe. In these systems, the downstream components use their decisions without human review, while the option order is set by upstream and can vary across calls. The loss in performance grows with the option set size, which reaches thousands in industrial-scale applications (Zhang et al., 2025; Qin et al., 2024), and errors compound in multi-step decisions (Deng et al., 2023; Sinha et al., 2026). We investigate two questions: how pervasive and harmful is order sensitivity in existing models, and how we can remove it while preserving the key advantages of decision models.

First, we characterize the order sensitivity of ten open- and closed-source models by their worst-case performance (Section 3). We find that order sensitivity is both pervasive and harmful. On challenging knowledge questions, all models we evaluate lose 13.5–64.2% of their average accuracy in the worst case (Figure 1). Furthermore, this effect grows with the number of options: on the same intent classification dataset, the OpenAI Decisions API’s worst-case loss jumps from 2.2% to 55.8% as the number of options increases from 4 to 151. Errors compound on multi-step decision tasks, with even the most robust model retaining only 53.8% of its success rate by the fifth step (Figure 2).

Second, we systematically compare eight methods adapted from prior work that address order sensitivity. We revisit methods from prior work spanning multiple categories: post-hoc calibration of the output distribution (Zhao et al., 2021; Zheng et al., 2024), training-time augmentation with permuted orders (Pradeep et al., 2023; Zhu et al., 2025a), test-time ensembling over orders (Wang et al., 2024a), and architectural designs (McIlroy-Young et al., 2024; Amit, 2026). By implementing them on a shared baseline decision model, we judge each method by its average and worst-case accuracy, and its training and inference cost (Section 5).

We find that tree attention is a surprisingly efficient and effective method. It offers order invariance in a single forward pass by processing options as parallel branches of a shared context. It does not lower average accuracy when used in training and loses only 1.1 points when applied to the baseline at test time. In comparison, post-hoc calibration and training-time augmentation have little effect; test-time ensembling costs multiple forward passes and scales poorly as the option set size increases; filtered ensembling suffers from high latency; and separate option encoding lowers average performance substantially. Additionally, we trained a 4B model using tree attention and show that its worst-case performance is better than or on par with existing models of comparable size (Table 3).

2 Definitions and Metrics

A dataset has NN items (questions). Item nn consists of a context xnx_{n} and a set of options 𝒜n={a1,…,aK}\mathcal{A}_{n}=\{a_{1},\dots,a_{K}\} of size KK, including a gold option gn∈𝒜ng_{n}\in\mathcal{A}_{n} (henceforth, we drop the index nn for simplicity). An option order is a permutation π\pi of {1,…,K}\{1,\dots,K\} that lists option aπ⁡(j)a_{\pi(j)} at position jj. Let Π\Pi denote the set of all K!K! possible option permutations. A decision model θ\theta reads (x,aπ⁡(1),…,aπ⁡(K))(x,a_{\pi(1)},\dots,a_{\pi(K)}) and returns a probability distribution pθ(⋅∣x,π)p_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x,\pi) over the options. We extract the answer a^​(π)=arg⁡maxa∈𝒜​pθ​(a∣x,π)\hat{a}(\pi)=\arg\max_{a\in\mathcal{A}}p_{\theta}(a\mid x,\pi).

Order sensitivity describes the extent to which a decision model’s predictions or performance vary with the ordering of options when the ordering carries no semantic information. Conversely, order invariance is the property that a model’s prediction remains unchanged under permutations:

pθ​(a∣x,π)=pθ​(a∣x,π′)∀a∈𝒜,π,π′.p_{\theta}(a\mid x,\pi)=p_{\theta}(a\mid x,\pi^{\prime})\quad\forall a\in\mathcal{A},\pi,\pi^{\prime}. (1)

We focus on the weaker but more practical property that the selected answer a^​(π)\hat{a}(\pi) is invariant under permutation:

a^​(π)=a^​(π′)∀π,π′.\hat{a}(\pi)=\hat{a}(\pi^{\prime})\quad\forall\pi,\pi^{\prime}. (2)

Metrics. We first define all metrics over the full set of option orders Π\Pi, and then propose efficient estimators that we use in practice. These metrics capture the different effects of order sensitivity on robustness and performance.

Average accuracy (AavgA_{\mathrm{avg}}) measures the mean accuracy across option orders:

Aavg=1N∑n=1N1|Π|∑π∈Π𝟏[a^n(π)=gn].A_{\mathrm{avg}}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{n=1}^{N}\frac{1}{|\Pi|}\sum_{\pi\in\Pi}\mathbf{1}\left[\hat{a}_{n}(\pi)=g_{n}\right]. (3)

Worst-case accuracy (AminA_{\mathrm{min}}) measures the share of questions answered correctly under all option orders:

Amin=1N∑n=1N𝟏[a^n(π)=gn∀π∈Π].A_{\mathrm{min}}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{n=1}^{N}\mathbf{1}\left[\hat{a}_{n}(\pi)=g_{n}\ \ \forall\pi\in\Pi\right]. (4)

Accuracy drop (Δ​A\Delta A) measures the degradation from average to worst-case accuracy:

Δ​A=Aavg−Amin.\Delta A=A_{\mathrm{avg}}-A_{\min}. (5)

Accuracy retention (RA{R}_{A}) is the share of average accuracy kept under the worst-case order:

RA=Amin/Aavg.R_{A}=A_{\mathrm{min}}/A_{\mathrm{avg}}. (6)

We use this metric when average accuracy varies.

Pairwise flip rate measures the fraction of pairs of option orders that yield different answers:

Flip=1N∑n=1N(|Π|2)−1∑{π,π′}⊆Π𝟏[a^n(π)≠a^n(π′)].\mathrm{Flip}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{n=1}^{N}\binom{|\Pi|}{2}^{-1}\sum_{\{\pi,\pi^{\prime}\}\subseteq\Pi}\mathbf{1}\left[\hat{a}_{n}(\pi)\neq\hat{a}_{n}(\pi^{\prime})\right]. (7)

Estimation. Evaluating all K!K! orders is infeasible for large KK. For each item nn, we therefore use a subsample Πn⊆Π\Pi_{n}\subseteq\Pi consisting of the KK orders given by the rows of a random Latin square over the options, which counterbalances position and option: every option appears exactly once in every position. We obtain the estimates A^avg\hat{A}_{\mathrm{avg}}, A^min\hat{A}_{\min}, Δ​A^\widehat{\Delta A}, R^A\hat{R}_{A}, and Flip^\widehat{\mathrm{Flip}} by replacing Π\Pi with Πn\Pi_{n} in the definitions above, i.e., by averaging over π∈Πn\pi\in\Pi_{n} and over pairs πs,πt∈Πn\pi_{s},\pi_{t}\in\Pi_{n} with s<ts<t. All reported numbers are these estimates. Since Πn⊆Π\Pi_{n}\subseteq\Pi, our worst-case accuracy is an upper bound (A^min≥Amin\hat{A}_{\min}\geq A_{\min}), so our estimates understate the true order sensitivity (see Table 9 for how tight the estimate is).

3 Order Sensitivity in Existing Models

This section quantifies the order sensitivity of existing decision models. We test 8 open-source decision models ranging from 1.7B to 27B parameters: Tacit 1.7B and 4B (Zhang, 2026a; Zhang, 2026b), d3-nano 2.2B (vLLM Semantic Router Team, 2026b), Kev 4B (Palmer, 2026b), Intern-Decision 4B (Zhu et al., 2026b), d3-mini 4.5B (vLLM Semantic Router Team, 2026a), and Elephant 9B and Mammoth 27B (Kirkby et al., 2026). Of these, d3-nano, d3-mini, Elephant, and Mammoth are top-ranking in their size cohort on the Jev Decision Index (multimodalart, 2026). We also test two closed-source models: TypeSafe AI’s Jev and OpenAI Decisions API.

Evaluation covers three task types representative of decision model applications, using the metrics defined in Section 2:

  1. 1.

    Multiple-choice question answering: ARC (Clark et al., 2018), MMLU (Hendrycks et al., 2021), and MMLU-Pro (Wang et al., 2024b).

  2. 2.

    Intent classification: BANKING77 (Casanueva et al., 2020), CLINC150 (Larson et al., 2019), and MASSIVE (FitzGerald et al., 2023).

  3. 3.

    Multi-step web tasks: Mind2Web (Deng et al., 2023).

Existing decision models suffer from order sensitivity. As shown in Figure 1, every tested model loses substantial accuracy under the worst-case order, with accuracy retention ranging from 35.8% to 86.5% on MMLU-Pro, 7.5% to 96.8% on MASSIVE, and 34.2% to 93.2% on Mind2Web. Larger models tend to be more robust, but scaling the model size does not remove order sensitivity effectively: Mammoth 27B loses only about 3 points less than d3-nano 2.2B on MMLU-Pro and Mind2Web.

The sensitivity grows with the option set size. To examine how sensitivity scales with the option set size, we vary the number of input options on CLINC150 and MASSIVE. Figure 2 shows that all systems start with little accuracy drop with 4 options, but many degrade sharply as early as when the option count rises to 10. To highlight two severe cases: the OpenAI Decisions API keeps 97.8% of its average accuracy with 4 options but only 44.2% with all 151 options of CLINC150; Intern 4B keeps 96.8% with 4 options but only 7.5% with 60 options of MASSIVE. This effect limits decision models deployed for settings with large option sets such as hundreds of intents, thousands of tools and APIs (Qin et al., 2024; Patil et al., 2024), or routing requests among >>40,000 skills (Kim et al., 2018).

The sensitivity compounds over steps. In multi-step tasks such as web navigation, a major application of decision models, small instabilities can surface and accumulate at every step; yet the effect of order sensitivity in such settings remains unexplored. On Mind2Web, we test models on 190 tasks with at least five steps. We find that the worst-case accuracy degrades over steps, and by the fifth step, eight of the ten models retain less than half of their average accuracy (Figure 2). The most robust model in the previous tests, Mammoth 27B, retains 88.8% of its average task success at step 1 but only 53.8% by step 5. We also measure the pairwise path flip rate, i.e., how often a model produces a different path when options are presented in a different order. We find that the flip rate increases steadily: by step 10, nine of the ten models flip with more than a 50% chance, and the most robust one flips its path with a 46.6% chance.

Together, these observations suggest that evaluations of decision models should report their robustness by measuring performance across multiple option orders rather than a single fixed order. The observations also call for methods that reduce order sensitivity.

4 Methods for Reducing Order Sensitivity

In this section, we review representative methods for reducing order sensitivity. We group them into four families according to where they intervene: post-hoc calibration, training-time augmentation, test-time ensembling, and architectural design. We summarize these methods in Figure 3, and provide a discussion of related work in Appendix A.

4.1 Post-hoc calibration

Calibration only changes how the KK output probabilities turn into an answer. Most methods rescale the log-probability of each position with parameters shared across items (Guo et al., 2017; Zhao et al., 2021), estimated either without labels (Zhao et al., 2021; Fei et al., 2023; Zhou et al., 2024b; Zheng et al., 2024; Lv et al., 2026) or from labelled data (Guo et al., 2017). We test one method of each kind.

Prior correction (PriDe; Zheng et al., 2024) estimates the model’s prior over positions from a few (typically 5%) items answered in several orders and divides it out of every prediction. While PriDe was originally proposed for the prior over option ID tokens, we apply it to positions.

Per-position temperature scaling assigns each position kk a temperature τk\tau_{k} and takes the answer distribution as a softmax over log⁡pk/τk\log p_{k}/\tau_{k}. The temperatures are fitted on labeled items from the target distribution.

4.2 Training-time augmentation

A model can pick up position preferences during training, and many studies offset the bias by augmenting the training data. Data augmentation shows each training example multiple times under different option orders (Pradeep et al., 2023; Zhu et al., 2025a); Appendix A lists further applications. We test one common form: training for several epochs where each epoch gives a new random option order for every question.

4.3 Test-time ensembling

Ensembling asks the model to answer the same question under different option orders and aggregates the answers into one. Typical aggregations include averaging the probabilities (avg) (Zheng et al., 2024; Raghavan, 2026), majority vote (vote) (Pezeshkpour & Hruschka, 2024), and taking a geometric mean (Zhang et al., 2026). Averaging over all K!K! orders makes the answer exactly order-invariant (Izacard et al., 2023; Zheng et al., 2024), but its factorial complexity makes it infeasible. Methods differ mainly in which orders they use, and we test three.

Random-permutation ensemble aggregates the answers over mm random orders (Pezeshkpour & Hruschka, 2024; Hou et al., 2024; Tang et al., 2024). It approaches the full K!K! average as mm grows, but for finite mm it is order-invariant only in expectation over the draw. We report the random ensemble with avg and vote.

Cyclic-permutation ensemble presents the question in the KK cyclic shifts of a start order (Izacard et al., 2023; Zheng et al., 2024). These shifts form a Latin square, the smallest set in which each option takes each position exactly once. AnyJev (Zhang et al., 2026) combines this design with the L0 reducer, which estimates the model’s prior over positions from the evaluation set and divides it out of each answer before taking the geometric mean (Appendix C). We report the cyclic ensemble with both avg and L0.

Filtered cyclic-permutation ensemble first filters out a shortlist of options and then ensembles over the shortlist only (Deng et al., 2023; Tang et al., 2024; Zhu et al., 2025b; Blankenstein et al., 2026). We follow Runoff (Huang et al., 2026) which formalizes this design for decision models. At the filter stage, the model scores each option individually. The filter then selects a set CC of at least kmink_{\min} top-pp options whose combined probability mass reaches pp. Since each option is scored independently, this stage is order-invariant. At the ensemble stage, a cyclic-permutation ensemble over CC produces the final answer. The method costs |C|+1|C|{+}1 passes in two sequential steps, where kmin≤|C|≤Kk_{\min}\leq|C|\leq K.

4.4 Architectural designs

Separate option encoding encodes each option in isolation from the question and other options, and then symmetrically scores all option encodings (Reimers & Gurevych, 2019; Karpukhin et al., 2020; Khattab & Zaharia, 2020; Humeau et al., 2020). Among decision models, Jeva (Li & Wang, 2026) implements this by using a shared encoder to encode the request and options independently, and then scoring each option encoding against the question encoding symmetrically. It guarantees order-invariance and allows individual option encodings to be cached and reused across requests.

Tree attention treats the options as parallel branches that share the context xx as a common prefix. Given xx and options a1,…,aKa_{1},\dots,a_{K}, Tree attention modifies the attention mask so that each token in aka_{k} attends to xx and to the preceding tokens of aka_{k}, but not to tokens of other options aj≠ka_{j\neq k} (Figure 3, bottom right). Variants of this idea have been explored (McIlroy-Young et al., 2024; Brown & McIlroy, 2025; Egressy & Stühmer, 2025) and are most prominently applied to speculative decoding (Miao et al., 2024; Cai et al., 2024). Some recent work applies it to decision models (Panisa, 2026; avbiswas, 2026; Amit, 2026); we describe each in Appendix A. Since each option is encoded independently of the others and at identical positions, the method is order-invariant by construction and requires a single forward pass for any KK.

4.5 Other approaches

We do not test other methods because they are less common or less practical for training a decision model. Appendix A reviews the other related work in full.
